title: Property-Based and Mutation Testing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of property-based and mutation testing and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—property-based test concepts—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study property-based and mutation testing with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you verify stated behavior with meaningful assertions, including edge and failure cases. In this lesson, focus on property-based test concepts and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A good test states the behavior it verifies and isolates the cause of a failure. Include boundary and error cases; coverage alone does not prove that assertions are meaningful. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect property-based test concepts with generating input data before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Property-based test concepts
items.text: A good test states the behavior it verifies and isolates the cause of a failure. Include boundary and error cases; coverage alone does not prove that assertions are meaningful.

items.title: Generating input data
items.text: Treat console input as untrusted text. Validate format and range before using it, account for token-versus-line reading, and give users a clear way to correct invalid input.

items.title: Invariants
items.text: Tests should state and verify observable behavior. Include normal, boundary, invalid, and failure cases; a high coverage percentage does not show that assertions check the right outcomes. Apply that reasoning specifically to invariants and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Mutation testing concepts
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Add assertions for normal, boundary, and invalid cases; this plain-Java example requires no external test framework. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: design a check for property-based and mutation testing that includes a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case. Make the check fail visibly when the behavior is wrong.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
